scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Mahari dance traces its origin nearly a thousand years back to the daily ritual practices of the Jagannath Temple in Puri under the Ganga rulers of Utkala.
In the twelfth century, Chodaganga Deva codified the status of the dance by building dedicated residential localities for the maharis and establishing new ceremonies.
During the reign of Raja Ramachandra of Khurda in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, royal court patronage was added to the devadasis' temple duties.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The term mahari derives from 'maha-nari', meaning 'great lady'.
The dance was a daily sacred ritual executed for the satisfaction of Lord Jagannath before his nightly slumber.
The maharis held the spiritual status of the deity's spouse, maintaining high social esteem in earlier centuries where elite families dedicated their daughters to this sacred duty.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Mahari dance is inextricably linked to Odissi music, the classical music tradition of Odisha.
Performances feature the singing and enactment of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda set to traditional Odissi ragas and talas.
The pulse is traditional Odissi talas.
Vocal renditions of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda performed using the traditional ragas and talas of Odissi classical music.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Originally performed inside the sanctum sanctorum of the Jagannath Temple in Puri during night rituals or during outdoor temple processions, the dancer was decked in special jewelry and decorated with flowers.
She performed while the deity was dressed in saris specially woven with verses from the Gita Govinda.
In contemporary settings, the dance is presented on modern theatrical stages.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historic and contemporary figures include King Chodaganga Deva of the 12th century, King Ramachandra of Khurda, Guru Pankaj Charan Das who spearheaded the modern stage revival, his disciple Rupashri Mohapatra, dancer Minati Pradhan (recipients of the Mahari Award in 2012), and Sashimani Devi, recognized as the last professional temple mahari.
The core tradition is centered in Puri, Odisha.
Originating from the devadasi institution of the Jagannath Temple under the Ganga dynasty, Mahari forms the root lineage of Odissi classical dance and gave rise to the Gotipua form.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Mahari dance is parent of Odissi: Mahari dance provided the historical roots and foundation for classical Odissi dance.
Mahari dance is parent of Gotipua: Gotipua originated as an offshoot of the Mahari tradition during its decline in the 15th and 16th centuries.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Mahari was a sacred temple ritual performed exclusively inside the sanctum sanctorum of the Jagannath Temple for Lord Jagannath by dedicated devadasis; outsiders should respect its sacred historical context and ritual origins.

scenes.title: Until next time
